parts.title: Joining a language exchange club
parts.context: A man phones a club to ask about practising French.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a language exchange club to ask about joining. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Hello, Lingua Club, Nina speaking.

script.speaker: kenji
script.text: Hello. I'm interested in joining your club, to practise my French. A colleague told me about it.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Wonderful. We have lots of French speakers. Let me take a few details first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller wants to practise French, so 'French' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Can I have your name, please?

script.speaker: kenji
script.text: Kenji Watanabe. That's W-A-T-A-N-A-B-E.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Thank you, Kenji. Is English your first language?

script.speaker: kenji
script.text: No, I grew up in Osaka, so my first language is Japanese. I've lived here for six years.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: And how would you describe your level of French?

script.speaker: kenji
script.text: I studied it for years at school, so people expect me to be advanced, but honestly I'd say intermediate. I can read well, but I find speaking difficult.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: That's very common, and it's exactly why people join. Why do you need French now?

script.speaker: kenji
script.text: My company is sending me to work in Geneva next spring, so I want to be confident by then.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: That's a good reason. And which evenings are you free?

script.speaker: kenji
script.text: Mostly Tuesdays. On Wednesdays I have a class, and on Thursdays I play football.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Then let me explain what we offer. We have three kinds of meeting. The conversation night is on Tuesdays at the Riverside Café, and it's free. You only pay for your own coffee.

script.speaker: kenji
script.text: That sounds ideal. What else is there?

script.speaker: nina
script.text: There's also a film club, which is held in the university library, in the small cinema room. We show a French film and talk about it afterwards. It starts at eight in the evening, and it costs four pounds.

script.speaker: kenji
script.text: And at the weekend?

script.speaker: nina
script.text: On Sunday mornings there's a walk. We meet at the old bridge, and we speak only French, or the language of the person we're walking with. It's three pounds, which pays for refreshments at the end.

script.speaker: kenji
script.text: I'd like to try the conversation night first. Do I need to book?

script.speaker: nina
script.text: No, just come along. Look for a table with a small French flag on it. And do bring a notebook, because everyone writes down new words.

script.speaker: kenji
script.text: Thank you. I'll see you on Tuesday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A textile museum
parts.context: A curator introduces the museum and some of its exhibits.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a curator giving an introductory talk at a textile museum. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Calder Textile Museum. My name's Alan Grant, and I'm the curator. I'll begin with a little history, then tell you about some of our best exhibits.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: The museum was founded in eighteen ninety-seven, but that was in a different building. It moved here in nineteen twenty-three, and the collection has grown ever since.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: This building was originally a wool warehouse, which is why the rooms are so large and the floors so strong. Many visitors expect it was a cotton mill, because there were so many in this region, but it was always used for wool.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: Our biggest challenge is light. Sunlight and even electric light slowly destroy the colours of old fabrics, so most of our rooms are kept quite dark, and we ask you not to use flash.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: We now have about twelve thousand items in the collection. Only about a tenth are on display at any time, so we change the exhibits every six months. This year we've also introduced something new: an audio guide, which is available in five languages. It's free with your ticket.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: Let me tell you about five of our favourite items. In the first gallery, you'll see a silk banner from the seventeenth century. It's so fragile that it is rarely on display, so you're lucky to see it today.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: Beside it is a cotton loom, which is the only item in the museum you may touch. Please do try the shuttle. Children love it.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: Upstairs, the wedding dress in the glass case was donated by a local family. It was worn by four generations of brides, and the donor's granddaughter still visits.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: Next to it, there's a wool blanket, made in the nineteen twenties. What makes it special is that it was stitched by schoolchildren, as a class project. Each square has the child's name on the back.

script.speaker: grant
script.text: And finally, the printed scarf in the last gallery. It came from India, and was brought back by a traveller in the eighteen fifties. The patterns were printed with carved wooden blocks. Please enjoy the visit, and do ask any of our guides if you have questions.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A poster about plankton
parts.context: Two marine biology students plan a poster.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two marine biology students, Imogen and Raj, planning a poster about plankton. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: imogen
script.text: Raj, I've put together a first version of the plankton poster. What do you think?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: It's a good start, but I can see two problems. The pictures you downloaded are low quality, and they'll look blurred when we print them at that size.

script.speaker: imogen
script.text: I know. I'll look for better ones. What's the other problem?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: There aren't enough sources. Dr Okoye said every claim needs a reference, and at the moment we only have two.

script.speaker: imogen
script.text: You're right. I'll add some. The title is fine, I think, and I don't think there's too much text.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: No, the text is fine. And the colours are easy to read. Where shall we print it?

script.speaker: imogen
script.text: At the university print shop. It's cheaper for students, but it closes at four on Fridays, so we'll need to be there before that.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Then we'll go on Thursday. Now, what's the main message? I think it's that plankton produce a lot of the world's oxygen.

script.speaker: imogen
script.text: Yes, about half, and that's what will surprise people. It's more important than the point that plankton are food for whales, though we can mention that.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: What shall we put in the middle? I think a diagram of the food chain would be better than a photograph, because plankton are too small to photograph clearly.

script.speaker: imogen
script.text: Good idea. A map of where they live is also possible, but a diagram is clearer.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: I did think about adding a short quiz for visitors, but it would take up too much space.

script.speaker: imogen
script.text: Agreed. A poster should be simple.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: How long do we get at the poster session? Is it five minutes each?

script.speaker: imogen
script.text: No, it's only two minutes per poster, so we'll need to be very concise.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Then we should decide who answers which questions. I'll deal with the methods, since I did the sampling on the boat.

script.speaker: imogen
script.text: Fine. I'll take the questions about climate, as I wrote that part. What do we do on Thursday, apart from the printing?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: I'd like us to practise the whole thing out loud, with a timer, and then ask a friend to listen.

script.speaker: imogen
script.text: Good. And before Friday I want to check all the references again, because we have to submit a list with the poster.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Perfect. Let's meet in the library at ten.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: spider silk
parts.context: A biology lecture on how spiders make silk and why people want it.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about spider silk. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about one of nature's most remarkable materials: spider silk. Weight for weight, it is stronger than steel, yet it is light and flexible.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Silk is made in special glands in the spider's abdomen. It is a liquid protein, which turns into a solid thread as it is pulled out through small openings called spinnerets. A single spider can make up to seven different kinds of silk, each for a different purpose.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Consider the orb weaver, which builds the familiar round web. The frame of the web, and the lines that go out from the centre, are made from a very strong silk. But the spiral that catches insects uses a different kind, which is sticky and extremely stretchy. It can stretch to several times its length without breaking, which helps the web to absorb the impact of a flying insect.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Not all silk is used for catching food. Some spiders wrap their eggs in a soft silk sac, and young spiders of some species use a thread to travel through the air. They let out a line of silk, and the wind carries them away, a method known as ballooning.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Scientists would love to use spider silk in products. It could be used to make strong, light clothing, or in medicine, for stitching wounds. The trouble is that spiders cannot be farmed like silkworms. They are territorial, and they attack and eat one another when kept together.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So researchers have tried other approaches. They have inserted spider genes into bacteria, and even into goats, so that the animals produce the silk protein in their milk. The silk can then be collected and spun into fibres. It is an expensive process, but progress is steady.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Nature remains well ahead of us. No factory yet makes silk as tough as the thread of a garden spider. Next week we'll look at another natural material: coral.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
